text: The Asiatic lion, a population in the Indian state of Gujarat belonging to the subspecies Panthera leo leo, was first scientifically described in 1826 based on a specimen from Persia, with Johann N. Meyer proposing the name Felis leo persicus. Until the 19th century, this lion ranged from Saudi Arabia, eastern Turkey, Iran, Mesopotamia, and southern Pakistan to Central India. Since the turn of the 20th century, its range has been restricted to Gir National Park and surrounding areas. The Indian population has steadily increased since 2010; in 2015, the 14th Asiatic Lion Census estimated the population at 523 individuals over an area of about 20,000 km² (7,700 sq mi), and by 2017, it had risen to 650 individuals. In 2020, the population reached 674, and by 2025, it had increased to 891. In 2017, the Asiatic lion was subsumed into P. l. leo due to close morphological and molecular genetic similarities with Barbary lion specimens, though several scientists continue to use P. l. persica. A standardized haplogroup phylogeny supports that the Asiatic lion is not a distinct subspecies but represents a haplogroup of northern P. l. leo. Lions first left Africa at least 700,000 years ago, giving rise to Panthera spelaea (the cave lion), which became extinct around 14,000 years ago and diverged from modern lions about 500,000 years ago. Pleistocene lion fossils have been found in sites such as Shishan Marsh (Jordan, ~250,000 years ago), Wezmeh Cave (Iran, 70–10,000 years ago), Nadaouiyeh Ain Askar and Douara Cave (Syria), and Batadomba Cave (Sri Lanka, Late Pleistocene, possibly extinct ~39,000 years ago). A phylogeographic analysis of mtDNA from global lion populations, including extinct ones like Barbary lions, shows that sub-Saharan African lions are phylogenetically basal, supporting an African origin with a probable center in East and Southern Africa. Lions migrated from there to West Africa, eastern North Africa, and via the Arabian Peninsula into Turkey, southern Europe, and northern India during the last 20,000 years, with the Sahara, Congolian rainforests, and Great Rift Valley acting as barriers. Genetic analysis of 357 samples from captive and wild lions reveals four lineages: one from Central and North Africa to Asia, one in Kenya, one in Southern Africa, and one in Southern and East Africa. The first wave of expansion occurred about 118,000 years ago from East Africa into West Asia, and the second wave in the late Pleistocene or early Holocene from Southern Africa toward East Africa. The Asiatic lion is genetically closer to North and West African lions than to East and Southern African lions, with the two groups diverging about 186,000–128,000 years ago. Gene flow between Asiatic and North African lions was interrupted during the Holocene due to the extinction of lions in Western Eurasia and the Middle East. Asiatic lions are less genetically diverse than African lions, likely due to a founder effect in the Gir Forest remnant population. Their fur ranges from ruddy-tawny to sandy or buffish grey, often with black speckling and a silvery sheen; males have only moderate mane growth, with the mane on the cheeks and throat being only 10 cm (4 in) long. About half of Gir forest male skulls have divided infraorbital foramina, compared to one on each side in African lions; the sagittal crest is more developed, the post-orbital area is shorter, and the tail tuft is larger with less inflated auditory bullae. The most striking morphological feature is a longitudinal fold of skin along the belly. Males stand up to 107–120 cm (42–47 in) tall, females 80–107 cm (31.5–42 in); two Gir lions measured 1.98 m (6 ft 6 in) head to body with a tail of 0.79–0.89 m (31–35 in), totaling 2.82–2.87 m (9 ft 3 in – 9 ft 5 in); the confirmed total length of a male is 2.92 m (9 ft 7 in), with a record of 3.10 m (10 ft 2 in) allegedly by Emperor Jahangir in the 1620s. In 1841, Austen Henry Layard described a large, dark brown lion in Khuzestan, Iran; in 1935, a British admiral claimed to have seen a maneless lion near Quetta. In 1965, a 1,412.1 km² (545.2 sq mi) area in Saurashtra's Gir forest was declared a sanctuary, and a national park of 258.71 km² (99.89 sq mi) was established, with only Maldharis allowed to graze livestock in the surrounding sanctuary. The lions inhabit the two hill systems of Gir and Girnar, which contain tropical and subtropical dry broadleaf forests, thorny forests, and savannas. Five protected areas exist: Gir Sanctuary, Gir National Park, Pania Sanctuary, Mitiyala Sanctuary, and Girnar Sanctuary. The first three form the Gir Conservation Area (1,452 km² or 561 sq mi), the core habitat, while Mitiyala and Girnar protect satellite areas within dispersal distance. An additional sanctuary is being established in Barda Wildlife Sanctuary. The drier eastern part receives about 650 mm (26 in) of rainfall annually, while the west receives about 1,000 mm (39 in). The population recovered from near extinction to 411 individuals by 2010, with about 105 lions living outside the Gir forest, representing a quarter of the total. Dispersing sub-adults established new territories, increasing the satellite population since 1995. By 2015, the population was estimated at 523 individuals, inhabiting 7,000 km² (2,700 sq mi) in the Saurashtra region, comprising 109 adult males, 201 adult females, and 213 cubs. In 2017, the census revealed about 650 individuals. By 2020, at least six satellite populations had spread to eight districts in Gujarat, with 104 living near the coast; lions in coastal and coastal-to-Gir areas have larger ranges. Approximately 300–325 lions lived within the Gir preserve, with the remainder spread across Amreli, Bhavnagar, Gir Somnath, and the sanctuaries of Girnar, Mitiyala, and Pania, as well as outside protected zones. In 2024 and 2025, lions began swimming to Diu Island, separated by a narrow channel, prompting their relocation to Gujarat by the Diu administration due to human safety concerns, despite conservationist opposition. During the Holocene, from about 6,500 years ago and possibly as early as 8,000 years ago, lions colonized Southeast Europe (including Bulgaria and Greece) and parts of Central Europe (Hungary, Ukraine), with remains indicating no difference from modern Asiatic lions. Historical records suggest lions became extinct in Europe during Classical antiquity, though survival into the Middle Ages in Ukraine is possible. The Asiatic lion once occurred in Arabia, the Levant, Mesopotamia, and Baluchistan; in South Caucasus, it was known since the Holocene and became extinct in the 10th century. It survived in regions near Mesopotamia and Syria until the early 1870s and was extinct in Saudi Arabia and Turkey by the late 19th century, with the last lion in Iraq killed in 1918. In Iran, it ranged from the Khuzestan Plain to Fars province below 2,000 m (6,600 ft), with sightings in the 1870s limited to the western Zagros slopes and south of Shiraz; the last lions were sighted in 1941 between Shiraz and Jahrom and in 1942 about 65 km (40 mi) northwest of Dezful; a lioness's corpse was found in 1944 on the Karun River. In India, the lion once occurred in Sind, Bahawalpur, Punjab, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana, Bihar, and as far east as Palamau and Rewa in Madhya Pradesh, and as far south as the Narmada River. Reginald Innes Pocock assumed it arrived from Europe via Balochistan. Heavy hunting by British colonial officers and Indian rulers led to local extirpation; lions were exterminated in Palamau by 1814, in Baroda, Hariana, and Ahmedabad in the 1830s, in Kot Diji and Damoh in the 1840s, and during the 1857 Rebellion, a British officer shot 300 lions. The last lions of Gwalior and Rewah were shot in the 1860s, one near Allahabad in 1866, and the last of Mount Abu in 1872. By the late 1870s, lions were extinct in Rajasthan; by 1880, only about a dozen remained in Junagadh, and by the turn of the century, the Gir Forest held the only Asiatic lion population, protected by the Nawab of Junagarh. Male Asiatic lions are solitary or associate with up to three males, forming loose coalitions that rest, hunt, and feed together, displaying at shared sites; females associate with up to twelve, forming stronger prides with cubs, sharing large carcasses among females but rarely with males. Males and females usually associate only briefly during mating. Radio telemetry shows male home ranges vary from 144 to 230 km² (56–89 sq mi) in dry and wet seasons, while female ranges are smaller, between 67 and 85 km² (26–33 sq mi). During hot and dry seasons, they favor densely vegetated, shady riverine habitats where prey congregate. Coalitions of males defend territories containing one or more female prides, with three to four males showing a pronounced hierarchy, one dominating the others. Lions in Gir National Park are active at twilight and night, overlapping temporally with sambar, wild boar, and nilgai. They prefer large prey (190–550 kg), with domestic cattle historically a major component of their diet in the Gir Forest. Inside Gir National Park, lions primarily kill chital (50 kg), sambar deer, nilgai, cattle, and domestic water buffalo, with chital being the most common prey.

Coalitions of male lions defend home ranges that contain one or more female prides and hold territories for longer than solitary males; males in coalitions of three to four individuals show a clear hierarchy with one dominant male. Lions in Gir National Park are active at twilight and night, overlapping temporally with sambar, wild boar, and nilgai. They prefer prey between 190 and 550 kg, regardless of availability, and historically relied heavily on domestic cattle in the Gir Forest. Within the park, lions primarily kill chital (around 50 kg), sambar deer (especially during summer descents from hills), nilgai, cattle, and domestic water buffalo, with rare predation on wild boar and dromedaries. They typically kill prey less than 100 m from water, charge from close range, and drag carcasses into dense cover. They regularly scavenge at specific sites where livestock is dumped by Maldhari herders and, during dry, hot months, prey on mugger crocodiles near Kamleshwar Dam. In 1974, the wild ungulate population was estimated at 9,650, rising to 31,490 by 1990 and 64,850 by 2010, including 52,490 chital, 4,440 wild boar, 4,000 sambar, 2,890 nilgai, 740 chinkara, and 290 four-horned antelope. Domestic buffalo and cattle populations declined after resettlement due to removal from the conservation area, dropping from 24,250 in the 1970s to 12,500 by the mid-1980s, then rising to 23,440 by 2010. As prey communities changed, lions shifted predation to peripheral villages, killing an average of 2,023 livestock annually between 2005 and 2009 and an additional 696 in satellite areas. Dominant males consume about 47% more meat than coalition partners, though aggression increases with coalition size and kills remain small. Asiatic lions mate between October and November, with mating lasting three to six days, during which they do not hunt but only drink water; gestation lasts about 110 days, and litters consist of one to four cubs, with an average birth interval of 24 months, shortened if cubs die from infanticide or disease. Cubs become independent at about two years, and subadult males leave their natal pride by age three, becoming nomads until establishing their own territory. Dominant males mate more frequently, and during a 2012–2016 study, three females switched to mating with the dominant male; females mated with males from rival prides sharing their range, and these males tolerated the cubs, while only new males entering a territory killed unfamiliar cubs. Young females mated with males within their home range, while older females selected males at the periphery. The Asiatic lion exists as a single subpopulation, making it vulnerable to extinction from events like epidemics or fires; there have been poaching incidents and reports of organized gangs shifting from tigers to Gujarat lions, as well as drowning incidents after lions fell into wells. Before Maldhari resettlement, the Gir forest was degraded by livestock, which limited native ungulate populations; habitat recovery and wild ungulate increases followed resettlement. In October 2018, nearly 25 lions died, four from canine distemper virus, the same virus that affected Serengeti lions. Since the mid-1990s, about a third of the lion population has lived outside the protected area, increasing human-wildlife conflict, with local people using high-voltage electric fences to protect crops and some viewing predators as beneficial, while others kill lions in retaliation for livestock attacks. In July 2012, a lion killed a man about 50–60 km from Gir Forest, the second such attack in six months after a prior incident in Dhodadar. Panthera leo persica is listed on CITES Appendix I and is fully protected in India, where it is classified as endangered. In the 1950s, biologists recommended re-establishing a wild population in the former lion range; in 1956, the Indian Board for Wildlife approved Chandra Prabha Wildlife Sanctuary (96 km²) in Uttar Pradesh for reintroduction, and in 1957, one male and two females were released, though all 11 animals in 1965 disappeared. In the early 1990s, the Asiatic Lion Reintroduction Project evaluated sites, with Palpur-Kuno in Madhya Pradesh ranked as most suitable, followed by Sita Mata and Darrah National Park. Until 2000, 1,100 families from 16 villages and another 500 from eight were resettled, expanding the protected area by 345 km². Gujarat officials opposed relocation, fearing loss of Gir's unique status, and the matter went to the Indian Supreme Court, which in April 2013 ordered Gujarat to transfer some lions to Madhya Pradesh. Gujarat has continued to resist relocation. In 1977, Iran attempted to reintroduce lions to Arzhan National Park but faced local resistance and the plan was not implemented, though Iran continued seeking lions. In February 2019, Tehran Zoological Garden received a male lion from Bristol Zoo and a female from Dublin Zoo, with hopes for successful reproduction. Until the late 1990s, captive Asiatic lions in Indian zoos were interbred with African lions confiscated from circuses, causing genetic pollution; this led to the shutdown of European and American breeding programs for Asiatic lions, as founder animals were found to be hybrids. In North America, hybrid lions showed improved fecundity and reproductive success. In 2006, the Central Zoo Authority of India halted breeding of Indian-African cross lions, declaring them to have no conservation value. Now only pure native Asiatic lions are bred in India. In 1972, Sakkarbaug Zoo sold a pair of pure-stock lions to the Fauna Preservation Society, intended for the Jersey Wildlife Trust to start a captive breeding program. The Asiatic Lion International Studbook began in 1977, followed by the North American Species Survival Plan (SSP) in 1983. The North American captive population consisted of descendants of five founder lions—three pure Asian and two African or African-Asian hybrids—with high inbreeding coefficients. In the early 1990s, three European zoos imported pure Asiatic lions from India: London Zoo obtained two pairs, Zürich Zoologischer Garten one pair, and Korkeasaari Zoo in Helsinki one male and two females. In 1994, the European Endangered Species Programme (EEP) for Asiatic lions was launched, with the first European Studbook published by EAZA in 1999. By 2005, 80 Asiatic lions were kept in the EEP, the only captive population outside India, and by 2009, over 100 were present. The SSP had not resumed, as pure-bred Asiatic lions are needed to form a new founder population. Neolithic cave paintings of lions were found in Bhimbetka rock shelters in central India, dating back at least 30,000 years. The Sanskrit word for lion is 'सिंह' (siṃhaḥ), also the name of Shiva and the zodiac Leo; Sri Lanka is called Sinhala, meaning 'Abode of Lions'; Singapore's name derives from Malay 'singa' (lion) and 'pura' (city), from Sanskrit 'सिंह' and 'पुर'. In Hindu mythology, Narasimha, a half-man, half-lion avatar, is the fourth incarnation of Vishnu; Simhamukha is a lion-faced protector and dakini in Tibetan Buddhism. In the 18th book of the Mahabharata, Bharata deprives lions of their prowess. The lion features prominently in The Fables of Pilpay, translated into Persian, Greek, and Hebrew between the 8th and 12th centuries. The lion is the symbol of Mahavira, the 24th and last Tirthankara in Jainism. Lions are depicted on vases from about 2600 BCE near Lake Urmia in Iran. The lion was a significant symbol in Ancient Iraq and appears in a stone relief at Nineveh in Mesopotamia.
